name: First Fort Dearborn — officers' barracks (west range)

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FIRST FORT'S, NOT THIS COMPONENT'S. It opens on 17 August 1803, the day Swearingen's detachment reached the river at the bend where the fort was to be built (his journal, printed by Quaife), and closes on 16 August 1812, the day after the evacuation, when the fort was burned (data/exclusions.json fort_dearborn_first_1803). No source dates any single building inside it: the fort was built over the months after the arrival, and Whistler's draught of 25 January 1808 is the one day on which every component here is shown standing. It ends before the second fort's 1816 phases begin, so no scene date can resolve the two forts together.

position.symbolic_location: First Fort Dearborn, in the frame of Whistler's 1808 draught (register part 'west range'): E -44.2..-32.1 ft, N -24.1..+19.7 ft of the flagstaff's foot, facing east onto the parade. SEATED (T-2050) with the whole frame: the staff's foot at local E +1152.0, N +221.0, the frame's north on grid north; this record's origin is the box's NW corner, the footprint turned 90 degrees so its front faces east.
position.note: SEATED WITH ONE ORIGIN AND ONE BEARING FOR ALL FOURTEEN (T-2050), so no building moves against another. The box is the register's (data/traces/whistler_1808_fort_dearborn.json), read off the commandant's own measured draught at 4.52 px per foot from the 75 ft staff, good to about +/-1.1 ft an edge. THE ORIGIN: the staff's foot, which the register finds at the centre of the parade and within about a foot of the centre of both picket rows, is set on the fort site at local E +1152, N +221 - the Wright 1834 reading of the fort's place that docs/ROADMAP.md S5a cross-checks to 35 m against the modern landmark. That is the SITE, not the second fort's plan: John H. Kinzie (quoted on chicagology_prefire052) says the first fort 'stood upon the same ground as the last Fort' and 'was differently constructed', so the place carries over and nothing of the 1816 geometry does. THE BEARING: the frame's north is set on grid north, which is the register's own inference that the sheet's right is east, from the lake lettered down that margin; the sheet has no north arrow, so the bearing is inferred and adds nothing to it. The second fort's 8 degrees, read off Harrison 1830, is that fort's and is not borrowed. Grid and true north differ here by under half a degree. A CHECK, NOT A FIT: seated so, the outward row's west side stands about 124 ft from the 1812 river (data/terrain/epochs/e1830_natural/river.geojson) and the north-west blockhouse about 65 ft from it; the draught's red-ink '122 feet to River' from the west side and Wilson's '80 feet' from the north-west corner are figures of that size. Carry the datum's +/-20 m on the whole frame.

derivation.reason: Not by any of validate.py's methods (platted corner, traced waterline, street frontage): this is a fort-frame seat. It IS recomputed, by tools/read_whistler_1808.py --check (run by check.sh), which refuses this utm point and rotation unless they are what SEAT_LOCAL (local E +1152, N +221), SEAT_BEARING_DEG (0) and this record's FACING give the register box in symbolic_location, to 0.01 m (T-2050).

footprint.note: MEASURED: 43.8 ft along the parade face by 12.2 ft deep, the plan box the register reads for the west range. Its back wall stands on the inward row of pickets, as every range's does on the draught.

kind.note: Whistler's index no. 11, on the west side. Quaife: 'directly opposite were those for the subordinate officers'.

construction.note: Not stated on the sheet. Built by the garrison out of local timber in 1803; Quaife calls the factor's and agent's houses beside it 'two log houses', and the magazine is singled out as the one structure of brick.

stories.note: Whistler's index, note: 'the Barracks are two storeys high with shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade'. Quaife, reading the same sheet: 'two stories in height, with shingled roofs and covered galleries'.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. Two storeys of log, at the second fort's inferred 5.0 m. The register refuses a height from the folded elevations, which disagree with each other by 70 percent.

roof_type.note: The index says 'shingled Roofs' and each range's elevation, folded out over the curtain, draws a pitched roof with its ridge along the range. A gable is that roof; the shingles are not a parameter the archetype reads.

roof_pitch_deg.note: Unattested. The folded elevations are not drawn at the plan scale (the register's height cross-check FAILS), so no pitch is read off them. The second fort's ranges carry the same figure.

gallery.note: The same note: 'Galliaries fronting the parade'. Built along the parade face; nothing says how deep the gallery was or how it was carried, and the archetype's gallery is a typical one.

chimneys.note: The source’s identified 1808 folded front visibly shows 3 clear stack(s), checked in the actual drawing. Use that visible count for this first-fort occurrence with inferred continuity to 1812. No hidden or ambiguous stack is added. Exact position, height, section, brick treatment and survival unchanged to the scene date are not attested; the existing procedural set-out remains reconstructed. The complete 1812 total (including possible hidden fittings or schematic omissions) remains reconstructed; this is a conservative model choice to follow visible evidence, not positive proof of the historical total or absence. Source-visible counts remain explicit.

gallery_storeys.note: T-3041 upper gallery refinement. Whistler’s 1808 index attests two-storey barracks with 'Galliaries fronting the parade', without counting gallery levels. Currey’s 1912 retrospective bird’s-eye shows a covered upper walk with a vertical-pale railing over an open lower gallery on the visible courtyard ranges. Two levels are inferred for this member of the same garrison ranges, not claimed as a separately identified contemporary elevation of this individual facade. Gallery reach, post and floor sections, railing height and spacing, and roof fall are reconstructed; the 1808 folded elevations are not used as height scales. No surveyed placement or range footprint changes. Follow-up support placement: where explicit front rectangles exist, retain the old support count/rhythm but project a colliding post centre to the nearest solid pier clearing both storeys' rectangles and the existing casing/sill-horn envelope. This algorithm/placement and all sections remain reconstructed. Rail density/height and remaining occlusion are unresolved; no upper entrance or accessible gallery interior is asserted.

face_openings.note: Whistler’s actual 1808 upright folded front reads S/T/S/T/S in SCREEN order on both storeys (T extends lower, S is shorter). Source-relative horizontal fractions [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9] record a qualitative rhythm, not surveyed bay coordinates. Source count/relative silhouette is inferred; all metre set-out remains reconstructed: width 0.72 m, common 2.05 m head per existing storey, short sill 0.65 m and long-window sill 0.10 m. The single modelled lower door is the leftmost source-long bay in the upright crop, at reconstructed 0.02 m sill; this does not establish an actual door identity or entrance count. Upper long rectangles remain reconstructed glazed windows, not attested gallery doors. Existing rear rectangles retained. Long/short distinctions are weaker in the southern drawings; ignore lettering and ink noise. No plan, wall/storey height, position, bearing, roof, camera or date changes; 1808-to-1812 continuity remains inferred. Actual reviewed comparisons still differ.

function.note: Whistler's index no. 11, on the west side. Quaife: 'directly opposite were those for the subordinate officers'.

research_note: A RANGE OF THE FIRST FORT, BURNED ON 16 AUGUST 1812. Its plan is the commandant's measured draught and its two storeys and gallery are his own note; its wall height, pitch and stacks are ours, because the elevations he folded out over the curtain are not drawn to the plan's scale.
